lessons.title: Valvular disease: four lesions and the murmurs they make
lessons.body:
## Two ways a valve fails

A valve has exactly two jobs: open all the way, and close all the way. **Stenosis** is a failure to open, so the ventricle behind it has to generate enormous pressure to push blood through a small hole. **Regurgitation** is a failure to close, so a fraction of every stroke goes backward and the chamber behind it dilates to hold the extra volume.

Pressure overload makes a wall thicker. Volume overload makes a chamber bigger. That single sentence predicts most of what you will see on the echo report.

## Where you listen

| Valve | Location |
|---|---|
| Aortic | Right 2nd intercostal space at the sternal border |
| Pulmonic | Left 2nd intercostal space at the sternal border |
| Tricuspid | Left lower sternal border, 4th to 5th space |
| Mitral | 5th space at the midclavicular line, the apex |

High-pitched sounds, meaning most murmurs, use the **diaphragm**. Low-pitched sounds, meaning S3, S4, and the mitral stenosis rumble, use the **bell** pressed lightly.

## Aortic stenosis

A harsh **crescendo-decrescendo systolic** murmur at the right upper sternal border that **radiates to the carotids**. The carotid upstroke is late and weak, which is the finding that separates it from an innocent flow murmur.

It is a pressure-overload lesion, so the left ventricle hypertrophies, becomes stiff, and generates an **S4**. In older adults the cause is usually calcific degeneration; a bicuspid valve produces the same thing twenty years earlier.

The symptom triad is **angina, syncope, and heart failure**, and once symptoms start, untreated survival is roughly `5 years` with angina, `3 years` with syncope, and `2 years` with heart failure. Severe means a valve area under `1.0 cm2` or a mean gradient over `40 mmHg`.

> **Trap:** Severe aortic stenosis is preload dependent, because a fixed small orifice means stroke volume cannot rise. Nitroglycerin for chest pain in this patient can drop the blood pressure through the floor.

## Aortic regurgitation

A soft **early diastolic decrescendo** murmur at the left sternal border, best heard **sitting up, leaning forward, at end-expiration**. It is easy to miss because it is quiet and blends into the background.

The chronic form is a volume-overload lesion, so the ventricle dilates and the pulse pressure widens dramatically, giving a bounding, collapsing pulse and a systolic pressure that can read `170/40`.

**Acute aortic regurgitation** is a different disease: aortic dissection or endocarditis blows the valve open with no time to dilate. The murmur is short and soft, the pulse pressure is **not** wide, and the patient is tachycardic and in flash pulmonary edema. It is a surgical emergency.

## Mitral stenosis

An **opening snap** followed by a low-pitched **mid-diastolic rumble at the apex**, best with the bell in the left lateral decubitus position. The cause is almost always rheumatic heart disease.

The obstruction is upstream of the ventricle, so the **left atrium** takes the pressure: it dilates, fibrillates, throws clots, and backs pressure into the lungs. The classic presentations are new atrial fibrillation, hemoptysis, and a pregnant patient who decompensates in the second trimester when blood volume rises.

## Mitral regurgitation

A **holosystolic blowing** murmur at the apex **radiating to the axilla**. Chronic causes are myxomatous degeneration and prior rheumatic disease; the volume-overloaded left ventricle dilates and produces an **S3**.

**Acute mitral regurgitation** from papillary muscle rupture appears `2 to 7 days` after a myocardial infarction, classically after an inferior infarct because the posteromedial papillary muscle has a single blood supply. The patient crashes into pulmonary edema, and the murmur may be soft or absent because the pressure gradient equalizes fast.

## The one that mimics aortic stenosis

**Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy** makes a harsh systolic murmur too, but at the left lower sternal border, and it behaves backwards: it gets **louder** with Valsalva and standing, which reduce preload, and **softer** with squatting and handgrip.

> **Key:** Every other murmur gets softer when you drop preload. Only hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and mitral valve prolapse get louder, because a smaller ventricle brings the obstruction closer together.
keyPoints: Stenosis is failure to open and causes pressure overload with wall thickening; regurgitation is failure to close and causes volume overload with chamber dilation.
Aortic stenosis: harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur radiating to the carotids with a late weak upstroke, and the triad of angina, syncope, and heart failure.
Aortic regurgitation is an early diastolic decrescendo murmur heard sitting forward; the acute form has a narrow pulse pressure and is a surgical emergency.
Mitral stenosis is an opening snap plus an apical diastolic rumble and presents as atrial fibrillation, hemoptysis, or decompensation in pregnancy.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and mitral valve prolapse are the only murmurs that get louder with Valsalva and standing.

checks.q: A 79-year-old with exertional syncope has a harsh systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to both carotids. What does the carotid upstroke add?
choices: A bounding, collapsing upstroke confirms aortic stenosis
A late and weak upstroke supports aortic stenosis rather than an innocent flow murmur
The upstroke is unchanged in valvular disease
An absent upstroke indicates mitral regurgitation
checks.why: A fixed small orifice delays and blunts the arterial upstroke, which is what distinguishes true stenosis from a benign flow murmur. A bounding collapsing pulse is the signature of chronic aortic regurgitation, the opposite lesion.

checks.q: A murmur at the left lower sternal border becomes louder when the patient stands up from a squat. What does this suggest?
choices: Aortic stenosis, because standing increases the gradient
Mitral regurgitation
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, because reduced preload worsens the outflow obstruction
Tricuspid regurgitation
checks.why: Standing drops preload, shrinking the ventricle and bringing the septum and mitral apparatus closer, which worsens dynamic obstruction. Every fixed valvular lesion, including aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation, gets softer when preload falls.

checks.q: Three days after an inferior myocardial infarction a patient develops sudden pulmonary edema, hypotension, and only a soft apical systolic murmur. What is most likely?
choices: Chronic mitral regurgitation that was previously unrecognized
Acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture
Aortic stenosis
Mitral stenosis with new atrial fibrillation
checks.why: The posteromedial papillary muscle has a single blood supply and ruptures 2 to 7 days after an inferior infarct, flooding an unprepared left atrium. The murmur is soft precisely because pressures equalize quickly, so a quiet murmur does not exclude it.

lessons.title: S3, S4, and the sounds around the murmur
lessons.body:
## Two extra sounds, two different problems

Both extra sounds happen in diastole, and both are low pitched, which means the **bell**, pressed lightly, at the apex, with the patient rolled onto the left side. Press hard with the bell and you turn it into a diaphragm and hear nothing.

**S3** comes in **early** diastole, at the moment blood rushes passively into the ventricle. It is the sound of a floppy, volume-overloaded ventricle being slapped full. The cadence is **Ken-tuc-ky**.

It is normal in children, athletes, and pregnancy, where the ventricle is genuinely compliant and the volume is genuinely high. In an adult over about `40`, an S3 is the most specific physical finding for **heart failure with a dilated ventricle**, and it also appears in severe mitral and aortic regurgitation.

**S4** comes in **late** diastole, at the atrial kick. It is the sound of an atrium slamming blood into a **stiff** ventricle that does not want it. The cadence is **Ten-nes-see**.

That gives you a free diagnostic rule: an S4 requires an organized atrial contraction, so **an S4 cannot exist in atrial fibrillation**. Causes are anything that stiffens the left ventricle: long-standing hypertension, left ventricular hypertrophy, aortic stenosis, and acute ischemia.

> **Key:** S3 means a big floppy ventricle with too much volume. S4 means a small stiff ventricle with too much pressure. Dilated versus hypertrophied, in one sound.

## Splitting of S2

S2 is the aortic and pulmonic valves closing. Inspiration pulls more blood into the right heart, so the pulmonic valve closes a little later and you hear a **physiologic split that widens with inspiration and disappears with expiration**. That is normal.

Three abnormal patterns are worth recognizing:

- **Wide and fixed**, meaning split throughout the respiratory cycle with no variation, is the classic finding of an **atrial septal defect**, because the shunt equalizes right-sided filling regardless of breathing.
- **Widened but still variable** comes from anything that delays the right ventricle: right bundle branch block, pulmonic stenosis.
- **Paradoxical**, meaning split on **expiration** and single on inspiration, comes from anything that delays the left ventricle: left bundle branch block, severe aortic stenosis.

## Clicks and snaps

- A **mid-systolic click** followed by a late systolic murmur is mitral valve prolapse. Standing moves the click **earlier** and lengthens the murmur.
- An **opening snap** shortly after S2 is mitral stenosis. The shorter the gap between S2 and the snap, the higher the left atrial pressure and the **more severe** the stenosis.
- A **mechanical valve** makes a crisp metallic click. A muffled or absent click in a patient with a mechanical valve is an emergency: it can mean valve thrombosis.

## Rubs

A **pericardial friction rub** is scratchy, like walking on dry snow, often with three components in one cardiac cycle. Listen at the left lower sternal border with the patient **sitting forward at end-expiration**. Unlike a pleural rub, it continues when the patient holds their breath, which is the bedside test that separates the two.

## Pulses that carry information

- **Pulsus paradoxus** is an inspiratory fall in systolic pressure of more than `10 mmHg`. It is not paradoxical, just exaggerated, and it points to **cardiac tamponade** or a severe asthma exacerbation.
- **Pulsus alternans**, alternating strong and weak beats at a regular rate, indicates severe left ventricular dysfunction.
- **Jugular venous pressure** is read with the patient at `45 degrees`. A column more than `3 cm` above the sternal angle, which is roughly `8 cm H2O`, is elevated.
- **Kussmaul sign**, a jugular venous pressure that **rises** with inspiration, is the opposite of normal and suggests constrictive pericarditis or a right ventricular infarct.

> **On shift:** Nearly every S3 and S4 that gets missed is missed for one of two reasons: the diaphragm was used instead of the bell, or the patient was flat on their back instead of rolled left. Change those two things and the sound appears.
keyPoints: S3 is early diastolic passive filling into a dilated volume-overloaded ventricle; S4 is late diastolic atrial kick into a stiff ventricle.
An S4 is impossible in atrial fibrillation because it requires organized atrial contraction.
A wide fixed split S2 is an atrial septal defect; paradoxical splitting comes from left bundle branch block or severe aortic stenosis.
A shorter S2-to-opening-snap interval in mitral stenosis means higher left atrial pressure and more severe disease.
Pulsus paradoxus over 10 mmHg suggests tamponade or severe asthma, and Kussmaul sign suggests constriction or right ventricular infarct.

checks.q: A 68-year-old with long-standing hypertension is in atrial fibrillation. Which extra heart sound can be excluded on physiologic grounds?
choices: S3, because fibrillation prevents passive filling
S4, because it requires an organized atrial contraction
Both S3 and S4
Neither; both are possible
checks.why: S4 is generated by the atrial kick, which does not exist in fibrillation. S3 comes from early passive filling and is unaffected, so it remains entirely possible in this patient.

checks.q: A young adult has a systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border and an S2 that stays split through inspiration and expiration without varying. What does the split suggest?
choices: Normal physiologic splitting
Left bundle branch block
Atrial septal defect
Severe aortic stenosis
checks.why: A wide split that does not vary with respiration is the hallmark of an atrial septal defect, because the shunt keeps right-sided filling constant. Left bundle branch block and severe aortic stenosis produce paradoxical splitting, which is present on expiration instead.

checks.q: You suspect an S3 but hear nothing with the patient supine using the diaphragm. What should you change?
choices: Press harder with the diaphragm at the apex
Use the bell lightly at the apex with the patient rolled into the left lateral decubitus position
Listen at the right upper sternal border
Have the patient sit forward and exhale
checks.why: S3 is a low-frequency sound that requires the bell held lightly and an apex brought close to the chest wall by left lateral positioning. Pressing hard converts the bell into a diaphragm, and sitting forward is the maneuver for aortic regurgitation and pericardial rubs.

lessons.title: ECG and anatomy, second pass: the patterns that change the plan
lessons.body:
## Reciprocal change proves it is real

When one wall is injured, the leads looking at it from the opposite side see the mirror image. Inferior ST elevation in II, III, and aVF should come with **ST depression in I and aVL**. Anterior elevation should come with depression in the inferior leads.

Reciprocal change matters because it separates true occlusion from the things that mimic it. **Pericarditis** produces diffuse concave ST elevation with **PR depression**, and it has no reciprocal depression except in aVR. Early repolarization in a young patient has none either.

## The territories nobody looks at

**Posterior infarction** hides in plain sight. The standard twelve leads have no posterior electrode, so you see the mirror image in V1 to V3: **ST depression, a tall R wave, and an upright T wave**. Confirm it by moving leads around the back to V7, V8, and V9, where `0.5 mm` of elevation is diagnostic. It usually accompanies an inferior or lateral infarct.

**Right ventricular infarction** accompanies up to `40 percent` of inferior infarcts. Get a right-sided lead: **`1 mm` of elevation in V4R** confirms it. This patient's cardiac output depends entirely on preload, so nitroglycerin and morphine can cause profound hypotension, and the treatment for that hypotension is volume.

**Diffuse ST depression with ST elevation in aVR** is a pattern, not a wall. It suggests left main or severe three-vessel disease, or global subendocardial ischemia from anything that starves the whole myocardium.

## Occlusion patterns without ST elevation

Two patterns identify a critically threatened left anterior descending artery in a patient whose ECG does not meet STEMI criteria:

- **Wellens syndrome**: deeply inverted or biphasic T waves in V2 and V3, seen when the patient is **pain free**, with preserved R waves and no Q waves. It means a critical proximal LAD stenosis that has temporarily reperfused. A stress test can infarct this patient.
- **De Winter pattern**: upsloping ST depression at the J point in the precordial leads with **tall, symmetric, peaked T waves**. It is treated as an LAD occlusion equivalent.

**Hyperacute T waves**, broad and symmetric and disproportionately tall, are the earliest change of all, often before any ST elevation exists.

## When the baseline is already abnormal

A left bundle branch block or a paced rhythm changes the ST segments on its own, so you cannot read elevation at face value. The **Sgarbossa criteria** tell you what still counts:

- **Concordant ST elevation of `1 mm` or more**, meaning elevation in a lead whose QRS also points up, scores `5` points and is highly specific.
- **Concordant ST depression of `1 mm` or more in V1 to V3** scores `3`.
- **Excessively discordant ST elevation**, classically `5 mm`, scores `2`. The modified version uses a ratio of ST elevation to S wave depth of `0.25` or more, which performs better.

## Chamber enlargement

- **Left ventricular hypertrophy**: the S wave in V1 plus the R wave in V5 or V6 exceeding `35 mm`, often with a downsloping strain pattern in the lateral leads.
- **Right ventricular hypertrophy**: an R wave taller than the S wave in V1, with right axis deviation.
- **P pulmonale**: a tall peaked P wave over `2.5 mm` in lead II means right atrial enlargement.
- **P mitrale**: a wide notched P in lead II means left atrial enlargement, which is why it accompanies mitral stenosis.

## Axis and intervals, quickly

Normal axis runs `-30` to `+90` degrees. Look at leads I and aVF: both upright is normal, I up with aVF down is left axis deviation, I down with aVF up is right axis deviation.

Intervals: PR `120 to 200 ms`, QRS under `120 ms`, corrected QT under `440 ms` in men and `460 ms` in women. A QTc over `500 ms` is the threshold where torsades risk climbs sharply.

## The athlete's ECG

Endurance training produces findings that look alarming and are not: sinus bradycardia into the `40s`, sinus arrhythmia, first-degree AV block, Mobitz type I, early repolarization, and isolated voltage criteria for hypertrophy.

What is **not** normal in an athlete and demands evaluation: T-wave inversion beyond lead V1, ST depression, pathologic Q waves, complete left bundle branch block, a QTc of `470 ms` or more in men or `480 ms` or more in women, and any ventricular arrhythmia.

> **Trap:** The single most dangerous ECG habit is calling a normal-looking tracing reassuring. A completely normal ECG does not exclude acute coronary syndrome, and serial tracings exist because occlusion evolves.
keyPoints: Reciprocal ST depression supports true occlusion; pericarditis gives diffuse concave elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal change.
Posterior infarct appears as ST depression with tall R waves in V1 to V3, confirmed by 0.5 mm elevation in V7 to V9.
Right ventricular infarct is confirmed by 1 mm elevation in V4R and is preload dependent, so nitroglycerin is dangerous and volume is the treatment.
Wellens T waves and the de Winter pattern identify a critically threatened LAD without meeting STEMI criteria.
Sgarbossa: concordant 1 mm elevation scores 5, concordant depression in V1 to V3 scores 3, and excessive discordance scores 2.

checks.q: A patient has 2 mm of ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves and upright T waves, plus ST elevation in II, III, and aVF. What is the best next step?
choices: Call it anterior ischemia and treat medically
Obtain posterior leads V7 to V9 to confirm a posterior infarct accompanying the inferior infarct
Repeat the ECG in one hour
Diagnose pericarditis
checks.why: Anterior ST depression with tall R waves is the mirror image of posterior injury, and posterior leads confirm it with 0.5 mm of elevation. Treating it as anterior ischemia or waiting an hour delays reperfusion for what is actually a large infarct.

checks.q: A pain-free patient has deeply biphasic T waves in V2 and V3 with preserved R waves and no Q waves. What does this mean?
choices: Old anterior infarct with no acute significance
Wellens syndrome, indicating critical proximal LAD stenosis, and stress testing is dangerous
Benign early repolarization
Left ventricular hypertrophy with strain
checks.why: Preserved R waves without Q waves mean the myocardium is still alive but the artery is critically narrowed and temporarily reperfused. Exercise stress in this state can precipitate the infarct the pattern is warning about.

checks.q: A 21-year-old collegiate distance runner has a resting heart rate of 44, first-degree AV block, and voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy. He is asymptomatic. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: All three are recognized training adaptations and need no further workup on their own
Isolated voltage criteria mandate evaluation for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
First-degree AV block in an athlete requires pacing evaluation
A heart rate of 44 is always pathologic
checks.why: Sinus bradycardia, first-degree block, and isolated voltage criteria are expected consequences of endurance training. The findings that demand evaluation are T-wave inversion beyond V1, ST depression, pathologic Q waves, and marked QT prolongation.

lessons.title: Pulmonary function tests: obstructive versus restrictive
lessons.body:
## Two numbers and a ratio

Spirometry asks the patient to inhale maximally and then blow out as hard and long as possible. Two measurements come out.

- **FVC**, forced vital capacity, is the total volume exhaled.
- **FEV1**, forced expiratory volume in one second, is how much of it came out in the first second.

The **FEV1/FVC ratio** is the whole game. A healthy adult blows out about `75 to 80 percent` of their vital capacity in the first second.

## Obstruction: air cannot get out fast

Narrowed or collapsible airways slow the exhale. FEV1 falls a lot, FVC falls a little or not at all, and the ratio drops. **An FEV1/FVC below `0.70` after a bronchodilator defines obstruction.**

Severity is then graded on FEV1 as a percentage of predicted: `80 percent` or more is mild, `50 to 79` moderate, `30 to 49` severe, and under `30` very severe.

**Reversibility** separates asthma from COPD. Give a bronchodilator and repeat: an increase in FEV1 or FVC of at least `12 percent` **and** at least `200 mL` is a significant response, which points to asthma. COPD improves incompletely or not at all.

## Restriction: the lungs cannot get big

Something stops the lungs from filling: stiff lung tissue, a stiff chest wall, a large abdomen, or weak muscles. FEV1 and FVC both fall together, so the **ratio stays normal or even rises above `0.80`**.

> **Trap:** Spirometry can only *suggest* restriction. Confirming it requires **total lung capacity**, measured by body plethysmography or gas dilution, and a TLC below `80 percent` of predicted is the actual definition. A low FVC alone can be produced by poor effort or by severe air trapping.

## DLCO: the test that sorts the look-alikes

The diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide measures how well gas crosses from alveolus to capillary. It falls whenever the membrane or the capillary bed is destroyed.

| Pattern | Ratio | DLCO |
|---|---|---|
| Asthma | Low | Normal or high |
| Emphysema | Low | **Low** |
| Chronic bronchitis | Low | Often normal |
| Interstitial fibrosis | Normal or high | **Low** |
| Obesity, kyphoscoliosis, neuromuscular | Normal or high | Normal |

That table does most of the work. Obstruction with a preserved DLCO is asthma; obstruction with a destroyed DLCO is emphysema. Restriction with a low DLCO is lung tissue disease; restriction with a normal DLCO is a problem outside the lung.

## The flow-volume loop

The loop plots flow against volume, and its shape is a picture of the disease.

- **Obstruction** scoops the expiratory limb into a concave shape as small airways collapse.
- **Restriction** produces a narrow, tall loop shifted toward low volumes.
- **Fixed upper airway obstruction**, such as a tracheal stenosis, **flattens both limbs**.
- **Variable extrathoracic obstruction**, such as vocal cord dysfunction, flattens the **inspiratory** limb only.
- **Variable intrathoracic obstruction** flattens the **expiratory** limb only.

That last group matters because vocal cord dysfunction is repeatedly treated as refractory asthma, sometimes for years.

## What you actually use in an emergency department

Full pulmonary function testing does not happen during an exacerbation. **Peak expiratory flow** does, and it is compared with the patient's personal best rather than a population value.

Below `50 percent` of personal best marks a severe exacerbation. Below `33 percent` is life-threatening. Peak flow is effort dependent and reflects large airways, so a patient too breathless to perform it is telling you the answer without blowing into anything.

> **On shift:** A patient whose peak flow does not improve after three bronchodilator treatments, or who is becoming quiet and drowsy, is heading toward respiratory failure regardless of what the number says.
keyPoints: FEV1/FVC below 0.70 after a bronchodilator defines obstruction; severity is then graded on FEV1 percent predicted.
A bronchodilator response of at least 12 percent and 200 mL points to asthma rather than COPD.
Restriction shows a normal or high ratio with both values reduced, and is confirmed only by a total lung capacity below 80 percent predicted.
DLCO separates asthma from emphysema and lung-tissue restriction from chest-wall restriction.
Flattening of both flow-volume limbs means fixed upper airway obstruction; inspiratory-only flattening suggests vocal cord dysfunction.

checks.q: Spirometry shows FEV1 62 percent predicted, FVC 64 percent predicted, and FEV1/FVC 0.82. What does this pattern indicate?
choices: Obstruction
A restrictive pattern that must be confirmed with total lung capacity
A mixed pattern
A normal study
checks.why: Both volumes falling together with a preserved or elevated ratio is the restrictive pattern, but spirometry cannot confirm it. Total lung capacity below 80 percent of predicted is the actual definition, since poor effort can produce the same tracing.

checks.q: Two patients both have an FEV1/FVC of 0.55. One has a DLCO of 42 percent predicted, the other 105 percent. What is the most likely pair of diagnoses?
choices: Both have asthma
Emphysema in the first, asthma in the second
Asthma in the first, emphysema in the second
Pulmonary fibrosis in the first, obesity in the second
checks.why: Emphysema destroys alveolar capillary surface area, so obstruction with a low DLCO points there, while asthma narrows airways without destroying membrane and leaves DLCO normal or high. Fibrosis and obesity produce restrictive ratios, not an FEV1/FVC of 0.55.

checks.q: A patient carries a diagnosis of severe asthma but never improves with bronchodilators. The flow-volume loop shows a flattened inspiratory limb with a normal expiratory limb. What does this suggest?
choices: Fixed tracheal stenosis
Emphysema
Variable extrathoracic obstruction such as vocal cord dysfunction
Restrictive lung disease
checks.why: An extrathoracic lesion is pulled closed during inspiration and pushed open during expiration, flattening only the inspiratory limb. Fixed lesions flatten both limbs, and emphysema scoops the expiratory limb instead.

lessons.title: Mechanical ventilation: the settings, the waveform, and the alarms
lessons.body:
## The machine does one of two things

Every mode answers one question: does the ventilator guarantee a **volume** or a **pressure**?

- **Volume control**, usually run as assist-control, delivers a set tidal volume every time. Pressure varies with how stiff the lungs are, so a worsening lung shows up as a rising airway pressure.
- **Pressure control** delivers a set inspiratory pressure for a set time. Volume varies with compliance, so a worsening lung shows up as a **falling tidal volume**.
- **Pressure support** assists only breaths the patient starts. The patient sets the rate and the inspiratory time, so it requires an intact respiratory drive and is the standard weaning mode.

In assist-control, every breath the patient triggers receives the **full** set volume. A tachypneic patient triggering `35` times a minute gets `35` full breaths, which is exactly how breath stacking begins.

## Starting settings

- **Tidal volume `6 to 8 mL/kg` of predicted body weight**, and `6 mL/kg` if there is any suspicion of acute respiratory distress syndrome. Predicted weight is calculated from **height**, not from the number on the scale, because lungs do not grow with obesity.
- **Rate `12 to 16`**, adjusted to the carbon dioxide level.
- **PEEP `5 cm H2O`** as a default, higher when oxygenation is the problem.
- **FiO2 `100 percent`** initially, then weaned quickly to a target SpO2 of about `92 to 96 percent`.

Two safety numbers: keep the **plateau pressure under `30 cm H2O`**, and keep the **driving pressure**, which is plateau minus PEEP, under about `15`. Those two limits are what prevent the ventilator from injuring the lung it is supporting.

## The obstructed patient is a special case

An asthmatic or a COPD patient cannot get air **out**. Give them a normal rate and the next breath starts before the last one finished, air stacks, intrathoracic pressure climbs, venous return fails, and the blood pressure collapses.

So you deliberately slow everything down: rate `8 to 10`, a long expiratory time with an I:E ratio of `1:4` or `1:5`, and you accept a high carbon dioxide level as long as the pH stays above roughly `7.20`. That is **permissive hypercapnia**.

> **Key:** If an intubated asthmatic suddenly becomes hypotensive, **disconnect them from the ventilator** and press on the chest to let the trapped air out. Pressure should fall and the blood pressure should return within seconds. That single maneuver diagnoses and treats breath stacking.

## Reading the two pressures

**Peak pressure** is measured during flow and reflects resistance plus compliance. **Plateau pressure** is measured during an inspiratory hold with no flow, so it reflects compliance alone.

- **High peak, normal plateau** means a **resistance** problem: secretions, bronchospasm, a kinked or bitten tube.
- **High peak and high plateau** means a **compliance** problem: pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, ARDS, a mainstem intubation, or a distended abdomen.

That single comparison sorts most ventilator alarms into two piles before you have touched the patient.

## The alarms

- **High pressure alarm**: something is obstructing or something is stiff. Work the list above.
- **Low pressure or low exhaled volume alarm**: there is a **leak**. Circuit disconnect, a deflated or ruptured cuff, or an extubation that nobody has noticed yet.
- **Apnea alarm** in a spontaneous mode: the drive is gone. Sedation, a neurologic event, or fatigue.

## When an intubated patient crashes: DOPE

- **D, Displacement.** The tube is in the esophagus, in a mainstem bronchus, or out. Waveform capnography is the fastest check: a sudden loss of the waveform means displacement or arrest.
- **O, Obstruction.** Secretions, a mucus plug, a kink, the patient biting the tube.
- **P, Pneumothorax.** Especially with high pressures or a recent central line.
- **E, Equipment.** Circuit, oxygen supply, ventilator failure.

The response is the same every time: **take them off the ventilator and bag them by hand with `100 percent` oxygen**, feeling the compliance in your own hand while someone listens and suctions. Hand bagging removes the machine from the differential in about five seconds.

> **On shift:** Keep the cuff pressure between `20 and 30 cm H2O`, keep the head of the bed at `30 to 45 degrees`, and keep suction at the bedside. Those three things prevent a large share of ventilator-associated pneumonia.
keyPoints: Volume modes guarantee tidal volume and show worsening lungs as rising pressure; pressure modes guarantee pressure and show it as falling volume.
Start at 6 to 8 mL/kg of predicted body weight based on height, rate 12 to 16, PEEP 5, and keep plateau pressure under 30 cm H2O.
Obstructed patients need a low rate, a long expiratory time, and permissive hypercapnia with pH above about 7.20.
High peak with normal plateau is a resistance problem; high peak with high plateau is a compliance problem.
For sudden decompensation use DOPE and immediately disconnect and hand-bag with 100 percent oxygen.

checks.q: An intubated asthmatic becomes acutely hypotensive with a rising peak pressure. What is the immediate action?
choices: Increase the respiratory rate to improve ventilation
Disconnect from the ventilator and allow full exhalation while pressing on the chest
Give a fluid bolus and increase PEEP
Increase the tidal volume
checks.why: Breath stacking raises intrathoracic pressure until venous return fails, and disconnecting releases the trapped air within seconds. Raising rate, volume, or PEEP all add more air to a chest that cannot empty the air already in it.

checks.q: A ventilated patient's peak pressure rises from 28 to 46 cm H2O while the plateau pressure stays at 20. What does this indicate?
choices: A compliance problem such as pneumothorax or pulmonary edema
A resistance problem such as secretions, bronchospasm, or a bitten tube
A circuit leak
Inadequate sedation only
checks.why: Plateau pressure measures compliance with no flow, so an unchanged plateau excludes stiff lungs and points to airway resistance. A leak would lower pressures and trigger a low-pressure alarm instead.

checks.q: A 5-foot-2-inch woman weighing 240 pounds is intubated for pneumonia. How is her tidal volume set?
choices: 6 to 8 mL/kg of actual body weight
6 to 8 mL/kg of predicted body weight calculated from her height
A fixed 500 mL for all adults
Whatever volume keeps the peak pressure under 30
checks.why: Lung size scales with height, not with adipose tissue, so predicted body weight is used and actual weight would deliver an injurious volume. Plateau pressure, not peak pressure, is the safety limit that is kept under 30.

lessons.title: The pleural space: effusion, empyema, and pneumothorax
lessons.body:
## A film of fluid holding two surfaces together

The pleural space normally contains `10 to 20 mL` of fluid, enough to let the two layers slide but not enough to separate them. Surface tension in that film couples the lung to the chest wall, which is how the chest wall's outward spring keeps the lung inflated against its own elastic recoil.

Break the coupling and both structures go where they want: the lung collapses inward, the chest wall springs outward.

## Effusion

Fluid accumulates when production exceeds lymphatic clearance. On an upright chest film you need roughly `200 to 500 mL` before the costophrenic angle blunts; **bedside ultrasound detects about `50 mL`**, which is one of the reasons ultrasound has largely replaced the film for this question. On a supine film a large effusion layers out and simply makes the hemithorax look hazy, which is easy to miss entirely.

### Transudate or exudate

The first question after drainage is whether the pleura itself is diseased. **Light's criteria** call it an exudate if **any one** of the following holds:

- Pleural to serum **protein** ratio over `0.5`
- Pleural to serum **LDH** ratio over `0.6`
- Pleural LDH over **two thirds** of the upper limit of normal serum LDH

**Transudates** come from pressure problems with healthy pleura: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome. **Exudates** come from sick pleura: infection, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, tuberculosis, pancreatitis, rheumatoid disease.

### When a parapneumonic effusion needs a tube

An effusion next to a pneumonia is common and usually resolves with antibiotics. It becomes a **complicated effusion or empyema**, requiring drainage, when the fluid shows:

- **pH below `7.20`**
- **Glucose below `60 mg/dL`**
- **LDH above `1000`**
- A positive Gram stain or culture, or frank pus

Empyema means pus in the pleural space, and antibiotics alone do not cure it. It gets drained.

> **Trap:** Remove no more than about `1.5 L` at a single thoracentesis. Draining a chronically collapsed lung too fast causes **re-expansion pulmonary edema**, and the patient who came in comfortable leaves hypoxic.

## Pneumothorax

Pleural pressure at rest is about `-5 cm H2O`. Air entering the space brings it to atmospheric, and the lung recoils away from the chest wall.

- **Primary spontaneous** pneumothorax happens in tall, thin, young people, usually smokers, from ruptured apical blebs.
- **Secondary spontaneous** happens on top of existing lung disease such as COPD, and is far more dangerous because the remaining lung has no reserve.
- **Iatrogenic** causes include central line placement, thoracentesis, and barotrauma from positive pressure ventilation.

### Tension physiology

A one-way flap lets air in on inspiration and traps it on expiration. Pressure builds, the mediastinum shifts, and the **vena cava kinks**. The patient dies of **obstructive shock**, not of hypoxia, which is why the hypotension and distended neck veins matter more than the oxygen saturation.

It is a **clinical** diagnosis. You do not wait for a film. Needle decompression goes into the `2nd` intercostal space at the midclavicular line or the `5th` intercostal space at the anterior axillary line, which is preferred in adults because the chest wall is thinner there, and a **chest tube follows regardless**.

An open chest wound gets a vented seal or a dressing taped on **three sides**, so air can escape but not enter.

### Small ones

A small primary spontaneous pneumothorax in a comfortable patient can be observed. Air resorbs at roughly `1 to 2 percent` of the hemithorax per day on room air, and **high-flow oxygen speeds that up several times over** by washing nitrogen out of the blood and steepening the gradient that pulls the trapped nitrogen back in.

> **On shift:** On ultrasound, **absent lung sliding** raises the question and a **lung point**, the spot where sliding starts again, is essentially diagnostic. Present sliding at that spot rules out a pneumothorax there.
keyPoints: The pleural film of 10 to 20 mL couples lung to chest wall; breaking it lets the lung collapse and the chest wall spring out.
An upright film needs 200 to 500 mL of fluid to blunt the costophrenic angle, while ultrasound detects about 50 mL.
Light's criteria call it an exudate if the protein ratio exceeds 0.5, the LDH ratio exceeds 0.6, or pleural LDH exceeds two thirds of the serum upper limit.
A parapneumonic effusion with pH under 7.20, glucose under 60, LDH over 1000, or pus needs drainage, not just antibiotics.
Tension pneumothorax kills by obstructive shock from a kinked vena cava, is diagnosed clinically, and is decompressed before imaging.

checks.q: Pleural fluid returns with a protein ratio of 0.61 and an LDH ratio of 0.42. How is it classified?
choices: Transudate, because only one criterion is met
Exudate, because meeting any single Light criterion is sufficient
Indeterminate without a pleural pH
Transudate, because the LDH ratio is below 0.6
checks.why: Light's criteria are deliberately sensitive: any one positive criterion classifies the fluid as an exudate. Requiring all three would miss infections and malignancies that the criteria exist to catch.

checks.q: A hypotensive trauma patient has absent breath sounds on the right, distended neck veins, and tracheal deviation. What is the correct sequence?
choices: Obtain a portable chest film, then decompress
Decompress immediately on clinical grounds, then place a chest tube
Intubate first to improve oxygenation
Give 2 liters of crystalloid and reassess
checks.why: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis because the patient dies of obstructive shock during the time it takes to get a film. Positive pressure ventilation before decompression accelerates the tension, and fluid does not relieve a kinked vena cava.

checks.q: A thoracentesis is draining a large chronic effusion and 1.4 L has come off. The patient begins coughing. What is the concern?
choices: Pneumothorax from needle entry
Re-expansion pulmonary edema from draining too much too quickly
Vasovagal syncope
Hemothorax
checks.why: Rapid re-expansion of a chronically collapsed lung causes capillary leak and pulmonary edema, and cough is the typical early sign. Limiting removal to about 1.5 L per session is the standard precaution.

lessons.title: Pulmonary hypertension and the right ventricle
lessons.body:
## A pump built for almost no resistance

The right ventricle is a thin crescent wrapped around the left. It moves the same stroke volume as the left ventricle against about **one sixth** of the pressure, so it is built for volume, not for pressure. Give it a sudden afterload and it fails within minutes, because it has no muscle mass in reserve.

**Pulmonary hypertension** is defined as a mean pulmonary artery pressure above **`20 mmHg`** at rest, a threshold lowered from the older `25 mmHg`.

## The five groups

| Group | Cause |
|---|---|
| 1 | Pulmonary arterial hypertension: idiopathic, heritable, drugs and toxins, connective tissue disease, congenital shunts, HIV, portal hypertension |
| 2 | Left heart disease, which is by far the most common |
| 3 | Lung disease and hypoxia: COPD, interstitial disease, sleep apnea |
| 4 | Chronic thromboembolic disease, the potentially curable one |
| 5 | Multifactorial and miscellaneous |

Group 2 matters clinically because treating it with pulmonary vasodilators can flood a left ventricle that already cannot keep up.

## The spiral

When right ventricular afterload rises acutely, a predictable sequence follows and every step feeds the next.

1. The right ventricle dilates because it cannot generate more pressure.
2. The dilated right ventricle pushes the **interventricular septum into the left ventricle**, so the left ventricle cannot fill properly.
3. Left ventricular stroke volume and systemic pressure fall.
4. Falling systemic pressure reduces coronary perfusion **to the right ventricle**, which normally receives flow in both systole and diastole but now receives it in neither.
5. The ischemic right ventricle fails harder, and the loop closes.

> **Key:** In right ventricular failure the systemic blood pressure is not a comfort measurement, it is the right ventricle's coronary perfusion pressure. Letting it drift down is how the spiral starts.

## Managing it without making it worse

Everything in this list is a physiologic lever on pulmonary vascular resistance.

- **Avoid hypoxia, hypercapnia, and acidosis.** All three constrict the pulmonary vasculature and raise the afterload you are trying to lower.
- **Fluid carefully.** A `250 mL` bolus at a time. A large bolus dilates an already overstretched right ventricle and worsens septal bowing.
- **Norepinephrine early** to keep the systemic pressure, and therefore right coronary perfusion, up.
- **Inhaled pulmonary vasodilators** such as nitric oxide or epoprostenol reduce pulmonary resistance without dropping systemic pressure.
- **Avoid intubation if you possibly can.** Sedation drops systemic pressure, and positive pressure both reduces preload and raises pulmonary vascular resistance. Induction is where these patients arrest.

## Cor pulmonale, at the bedside

Right heart failure from lung disease shows itself on the right side of the body: **jugular venous distension, a parasternal right ventricular heave, a loud P2, a holosystolic tricuspid regurgitation murmur that gets louder with inspiration, hepatomegaly with a pulsatile liver, ascites, and dependent edema.**

On the ECG expect right axis deviation, an R taller than the S in V1, **P pulmonale** with a peaked P wave over `2.5 mm` in lead II, right bundle branch block, and T-wave inversions in V1 to V4.

## The medications, and two rules about them

Chronic therapy uses **endothelin receptor antagonists** such as bosentan and ambrisentan, **phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors** such as sildenafil and tadalafil, **prostacyclins** such as epoprostenol and treprostinil, and the soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator riociguat.

Two rules that come up in an emergency department:

- **Never interrupt a continuous intravenous prostacyclin.** The half-life is minutes and rebound pulmonary hypertension can be fatal. Even a line infection is managed without stopping the infusion.
- **Never combine a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor with nitrates.** The two act on the same pathway and produce profound hypotension.

> **On shift:** A patient with known pulmonary hypertension who arrives looking mildly unwell has very little reserve. Treat the small decompensation seriously, because the distance between compensated and arrested is short.
keyPoints: Pulmonary hypertension is a mean pulmonary artery pressure above 20 mmHg, and the right ventricle fails quickly because it is built for volume rather than pressure.
The death spiral is dilation, septal bowing into the left ventricle, falling systemic pressure, loss of right coronary perfusion, and worse right ventricular failure.
Hypoxia, hypercapnia, and acidosis all raise pulmonary vascular resistance and must be corrected first.
Fluids go in small 250 mL boluses, norepinephrine is started early to protect coronary perfusion, and intubation is avoided when possible.
Never interrupt a continuous intravenous prostacyclin and never combine a PDE-5 inhibitor with nitrates.

checks.q: A patient with severe pulmonary hypertension is hypotensive after a massive pulmonary embolism. Why is norepinephrine used early rather than fluid alone?
choices: It directly dilates the pulmonary vasculature
It maintains systemic pressure, which is the right ventricle's coronary perfusion pressure
It slows the heart rate to allow filling
It reduces preload to unload the right ventricle
checks.why: A failing right ventricle loses its normal systolic and diastolic coronary flow when systemic pressure drops, so supporting pressure interrupts the ischemic spiral. Norepinephrine does not dilate the pulmonary bed, and large-volume fluid worsens septal bowing.

checks.q: A patient on continuous intravenous epoprostenol arrives with fever and a suspected line infection. What is correct?
choices: Stop the infusion immediately and remove the line
Continue the infusion without interruption while treating the infection
Switch to oral sildenafil until the infection clears
Halve the infusion rate to reduce line use
checks.why: Epoprostenol has a half-life of minutes, and stopping or reducing it causes rebound pulmonary hypertension that can be fatal. The infection is treated around the infusion, and oral agents cannot substitute acutely.

checks.q: Why is intubation especially dangerous in decompensated right ventricular failure?
choices: Sedation drops systemic pressure while positive pressure reduces preload and raises pulmonary vascular resistance
Endotracheal tubes cannot be secured in these patients
Oxygen worsens pulmonary vasoconstriction
Hypercapnia lowers pulmonary vascular resistance
checks.why: Induction removes the sympathetic tone holding the circulation together while positive pressure simultaneously attacks preload and afterload, which is why arrest commonly occurs at intubation. Oxygen dilates the pulmonary bed, and hypercapnia constricts it.

lessons.title: Congenital heart disease at recognition level
lessons.body:
## One question first: is the baby blue?

Congenital lesions sort into two piles, and the sorting question is whether deoxygenated blood is reaching the systemic circulation.

**Acyanotic** lesions shunt **left to right**, sending oxygenated blood back through the lungs. They cause too much pulmonary flow, heart failure, and failure to thrive, but not cyanosis.

**Cyanotic** lesions shunt **right to left**, dumping deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation, so oxygen cannot fix it.

## The acyanotic four

- **Ventricular septal defect** is the most common congenital heart lesion. It makes a harsh **holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border**, and counterintuitively, the **smaller** the hole the **louder** the murmur, because a small hole makes more turbulence. Many close on their own.
- **Atrial septal defect** often goes unnoticed into adulthood. The murmur is a soft systolic ejection sound at the pulmonic area, produced by the extra volume crossing the **pulmonic** valve rather than by the defect itself, and the giveaway is a **wide, fixed split S2**.
- **Patent ductus arteriosus** makes a **continuous machinery murmur** below the left clavicle. Indomethacin closes it; prostaglandin E1 keeps it open when a baby needs it open.
- **Coarctation of the aorta** is an obstruction, not a shunt. Look for **upper extremity hypertension with weak, delayed femoral pulses**, a radiofemoral delay you can feel with two hands. It travels with bicuspid aortic valve and with Turner syndrome.

## The cyanotic five

The memory aid is the **five T's**: **T**etralogy of Fallot, **T**ransposition of the great arteries, **T**runcus arteriosus, **T**otal anomalous pulmonary venous return, and **T**ricuspid atresia.

**Tetralogy of Fallot** is the one to actually know. Four features: pulmonic stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, an overriding aorta, and a ventricular septal defect. The chest film shows a boot-shaped heart.

Its emergency is the **tet spell**, a hypercyanotic episode where crying or feeding drops systemic resistance and more blood shunts right to left. The child becomes deeply blue and the murmur gets **quieter**, because less blood is crossing the pulmonic stenosis.

Treatment is aimed at raising systemic resistance so blood goes to the lungs instead: **knees to chest**, which is why older children squat on their own, plus oxygen, calming, morphine, fluids, and phenylephrine if needed.

**Transposition of the great arteries** creates two separate circuits and produces cyanosis within hours of birth. The infant survives only while a mixing point stays open, so the drug is **prostaglandin E1** to hold the ductus open until surgery. Its main side effect is **apnea**, so be ready to support the airway.

> **Key:** Any cyanotic newborn in the first weeks of life may have a **ductal-dependent** lesion. Prostaglandin E1 keeps the ductus open and buys the time surgery needs.

## Two tests worth knowing

The **hyperoxia test** separates heart from lung: put the infant on `100 percent` oxygen and recheck the arterial oxygen. A lung problem improves substantially; a PaO2 that fails to rise above roughly `150 mmHg` points to a cardiac right-to-left shunt.

**Newborn pulse oximetry screening** compares a **pre-ductal** reading on the right hand with a **post-ductal** reading on a foot. A saturation under `95 percent` or a difference of more than `3 percent` between the two is a failed screen.

## Eisenmenger, and why timing matters

A left-to-right shunt left alone for years drives pulmonary vascular remodeling until pulmonary resistance exceeds systemic resistance and the **shunt reverses**. The patient becomes cyanotic, and at that point **closing the defect is contraindicated**, because the hole has become the only relief valve for a right ventricle that cannot beat the lungs.

## Innocent murmurs

Most childhood murmurs are innocent. The reassuring profile is **soft, grade 2 or less, systolic only, no radiation, changes with position, a normally splitting S2, and a well child**. A **venous hum** is continuous but disappears when the child lies down or the jugular vein is compressed.

> **Trap:** Any **diastolic** murmur, any murmur grade 3 or louder, a harsh or holosystolic quality, a fixed split S2, or a murmur with symptoms is never called innocent.
keyPoints: Acyanotic lesions shunt left to right and cause pulmonary overcirculation; cyanotic lesions shunt right to left and do not correct with oxygen.
Ventricular septal defect is the most common lesion and a smaller hole makes a louder murmur; a wide fixed split S2 means atrial septal defect.
Coarctation gives upper extremity hypertension with weak, delayed femoral pulses and travels with bicuspid valve and Turner syndrome.
A tet spell is treated by raising systemic resistance with knees to chest, plus oxygen, calming, morphine, fluids, and phenylephrine.
Ductal-dependent lesions are held open with prostaglandin E1, whose main side effect is apnea; a failed newborn pulse oximetry screen is under 95 percent or more than 3 percent difference.

checks.q: A 4-month-old with tetralogy of Fallot becomes deeply cyanotic while crying and the murmur becomes quieter. What explains the quieter murmur?
choices: The pulmonic stenosis has resolved
Less blood is crossing the pulmonic stenosis because more is shunting right to left
The ventricular septal defect has closed
Cardiac output has increased
checks.why: The murmur comes from flow across the pulmonic stenosis, so a spell that diverts blood through the septal defect instead makes it softer. A quieter murmur in this setting signals a worse spell, not an improving one.

checks.q: A cyanotic newborn's PaO2 rises only to 60 mmHg on 100 percent oxygen. What does this suggest?
choices: Primary lung disease such as pneumonia
A cardiac right-to-left shunt
Methemoglobinemia is excluded
Normal transitional circulation
checks.why: Oxygen cannot reach blood that bypasses the lungs entirely, so a failed hyperoxia test points to a cardiac shunt. Lung disease usually shows a substantial rise because the alveoli that remain can be recruited.

checks.q: An adult with a long-standing untreated ventricular septal defect is now cyanotic with clubbing. What has happened and what is contraindicated?
choices: Endocarditis; antibiotics are contraindicated
Eisenmenger syndrome; closing the defect is contraindicated
Coarctation; beta blockers are contraindicated
Heart failure; diuretics are contraindicated
checks.why: Years of pulmonary overcirculation remodel the pulmonary vasculature until resistance exceeds systemic and the shunt reverses. Closing the defect then removes the only outlet for a right ventricle that cannot overcome the pulmonary bed.

lessons.title: Extremes and exposures: exercise, altitude, diving, and vaping
lessons.body:
## What exercise asks of the circulation

At rest cardiac output is about `5 L/min`. Maximal exercise takes it to `20 to 25 L/min` in a healthy adult and past `35 L/min` in an elite endurance athlete.

How it gets there is worth knowing. **Stroke volume rises about `50 percent` and then plateaus** at roughly `40 to 60 percent` of maximal effort. Everything above that comes from **heart rate**, which is why maximal heart rate, crudely `220` minus age, sets the ceiling.

The tissues help too. The arteriovenous oxygen difference widens from about `5 mL/dL` at rest to `15 mL/dL`, because working muscle extracts far more of what arrives. Systolic pressure climbs while diastolic stays flat or falls slightly, since muscle arterioles dilate.

> **Trap:** A systolic pressure that **falls** during exercise is an ominous finding. It means the heart cannot raise output against the dilating muscle bed, which points to severe ischemia or an outflow obstruction.

**The athlete's heart** is a symmetric enlargement: thicker walls with a **normal or larger cavity** and normal filling. **Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy** is asymmetric septal thickening with a **small** cavity, abnormal filling, and often a family history of sudden death. That distinction is the entire point of preparticipation screening, because hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a leading cause of sudden death in young athletes alongside anomalous coronary origin, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, long QT, myocarditis, and commotio cordis.

## Altitude

Going up does not change the **fraction** of oxygen in air, which stays `21 percent` everywhere. It lowers **barometric pressure**, so the partial pressure of inspired oxygen falls with it. At about `18,000 feet` the pressure is half of sea level.

The body responds in stages. Peripheral chemoreceptors trigger hyperventilation within minutes, producing a **respiratory alkalosis**; the kidney then excretes bicarbonate over `24 to 48 hours` to let ventilation rise further; 2,3-DPG increases, shifting the oxygen curve right. Meanwhile **hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction becomes global** instead of local, raising pulmonary artery pressure.

Three syndromes come out of that:

- **Acute mountain sickness**: headache plus nausea, fatigue, dizziness, or insomnia, appearing `6 to 12 hours` after ascent above roughly `8,000 feet`. Stop ascending. **Acetazolamide `125 to 250 mg` twice daily** works by causing a bicarbonate diuresis, producing a mild metabolic acidosis that drives ventilation, essentially doing the kidney's acclimatization work faster.
- **High altitude cerebral edema**: ataxia and altered mental status. Descend immediately, give dexamethasone and oxygen.
- **High altitude pulmonary edema**: non-cardiogenic edema from patchy hypoxic vasoconstriction overloading the vessels that stayed open. It is the most common cause of altitude death. Descend, oxygen, nifedipine.

## Diving

Two gas laws explain almost everything.

**Boyle's law**, volume varies inversely with pressure, governs **barotrauma**. Pressure rises one atmosphere per `33 feet` of seawater, so the greatest proportional volume change happens in the **shallowest** water: the first `33 feet` doubles or halves gas volume. That is why pulmonary barotrauma and **arterial gas embolism** happen on ascent from shallow depths in a diver who held their breath.

**Henry's law**, dissolved gas is proportional to partial pressure, governs **decompression sickness**. Nitrogen dissolves into tissue under pressure and comes out as bubbles if the ascent is too fast.

- **Arterial gas embolism** presents **within minutes of surfacing**, often with immediate loss of consciousness or stroke-like deficits. `100 percent` oxygen and urgent recompression.
- **Decompression sickness** presents over minutes to hours: joint pain called the bends, mottled skin, or neurologic and vestibular symptoms. Same treatment.
- **Middle ear squeeze** is the most common diving injury by far, and nitrogen narcosis appears around `100 feet`.

## Smoking and vaping

Tobacco smoke carries roughly `7,000` chemicals. Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with `200` to `250` times the affinity of oxygen, leaving smokers with a baseline carboxyhemoglobin of `5 to 10 percent`. Smoke paralyzes cilia, and it tips the **protease-antiprotease balance** so neutrophil elastase digests alveolar walls, which is emphysema.

That same pathway explains **alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency**: a young non-smoker with emphysema at the **lung bases** plus liver disease.

**EVALI**, e-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury, emerged in `2019` and was linked to **vitamin E acetate** in illicit THC cartridges. It presents with dyspnea, cough, chest pain, fever, and prominent gastrointestinal symptoms, with hypoxemia and bilateral ground-glass opacities that characteristically spare the subpleural region. It is a diagnosis of exclusion after infection is ruled out, and it is treated with steroids and support.

> **On shift:** Ask about vaping separately from smoking, and ask specifically about THC cartridges. Patients do not consider vaping to be smoking and will answer no to the general question.
keyPoints: Exercise raises cardiac output from 5 to over 20 L/min; stroke volume rises about 50 percent then plateaus, and heart rate carries the rest.
A falling systolic pressure during exercise suggests severe ischemia or outflow obstruction.
Altitude lowers barometric pressure, not oxygen fraction; acetazolamide accelerates acclimatization by producing a bicarbonate diuresis.
Boyle's law explains barotrauma and arterial gas embolism on ascent; Henry's law explains decompression sickness, and both are treated with oxygen and recompression.
EVALI is linked to vitamin E acetate in THC cartridges and shows bilateral ground-glass opacities with subpleural sparing.

checks.q: A diver surfaces from 20 feet after holding his breath during ascent and immediately loses consciousness. What is the mechanism?
choices: Decompression sickness from dissolved nitrogen
Arterial gas embolism from pulmonary barotrauma, because the greatest volume change occurs nearest the surface
Nitrogen narcosis
Oxygen toxicity
checks.why: Boyle's law makes the proportional volume change largest in shallow water, so a held breath during ascent overexpands alveoli and forces gas into pulmonary veins. Decompression sickness develops over minutes to hours, and narcosis and oxygen toxicity occur at depth, not on surfacing.

checks.q: Why does acetazolamide help with acute mountain sickness?
choices: It dilates the pulmonary vasculature directly
It increases hemoglobin production
It causes a bicarbonate diuresis, producing a mild metabolic acidosis that drives ventilation
It blocks hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
checks.why: Hyperventilation at altitude creates an alkalosis that limits further ventilation until the kidney excretes bicarbonate, and acetazolamide does that job faster. Nifedipine addresses pulmonary vasoconstriction, and erythropoiesis takes weeks.

checks.q: A 19-year-old has one week of dyspnea, cough, fever, vomiting, hypoxemia, and bilateral ground-glass opacities sparing the subpleural region. Infectious workup is negative. What must be asked?
choices: Whether he vapes, specifically whether he uses THC cartridges
Whether he has traveled to altitude recently
Whether he has a family history of emphysema
Whether he has been scuba diving
checks.why: This is the classic EVALI presentation, and vitamin E acetate in illicit THC cartridges was the implicated agent. Patients routinely deny smoking while vaping daily, so the question has to name vaping and THC explicitly.

cards.front: What are the two ways a valve fails, and what does each do to the chamber behind it?
cards.back: Stenosis is failure to open, causing pressure overload and wall thickening. Regurgitation is failure to close, causing volume overload and chamber dilation.

cards.front: Where do you listen for each of the four valves?
cards.back: Aortic right 2nd intercostal space, pulmonic left 2nd, tricuspid left lower sternal border at the 4th to 5th, mitral at the apex in the 5th space midclavicular line.

cards.front: Describe the aortic stenosis murmur and the pulse finding that confirms it.
cards.back: Harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids, with a late and weak carotid upstroke. An S4 is common from the stiff hypertrophied ventricle.

cards.front: What is the symptom triad of aortic stenosis and what does each predict?
cards.back: Angina, syncope, heart failure. Untreated survival after symptom onset is roughly 5 years with angina, 3 with syncope, and 2 with heart failure.

cards.front: Why is nitroglycerin dangerous in severe aortic stenosis?
cards.back: A fixed small orifice means stroke volume cannot rise to compensate, so the lesion is preload dependent. Dropping preload with a vasodilator can cause profound hypotension.

cards.front: How do you hear aortic regurgitation, and how does acute differ from chronic?
cards.back: Soft early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border, sitting forward at end-expiration. Chronic gives a wide pulse pressure and bounding pulse; acute gives a narrow pulse pressure, tachycardia, and flash pulmonary edema.

cards.front: Describe the mitral stenosis murmur and the chamber that suffers.
cards.back: Opening snap followed by a low-pitched mid-diastolic apical rumble, best with the bell in left lateral decubitus. The left atrium dilates, fibrillates, throws clots, and backs pressure into the lungs.

cards.front: Describe the mitral regurgitation murmur, and what makes the acute form different?
cards.back: Holosystolic blowing murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. Acute papillary muscle rupture 2 to 7 days after an inferior MI causes flash pulmonary edema with a soft or absent murmur.

cards.front: Which murmurs get LOUDER with Valsalva and standing, and why?
cards.back: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and mitral valve prolapse. Reducing preload shrinks the ventricle, bringing the obstructing structures closer together. Every fixed valvular murmur gets softer.

cards.front: When in diastole does S3 occur, and what does it mean?
cards.back: Early diastole, during rapid passive filling into a dilated volume-overloaded ventricle. Cadence Ken-tuc-ky. Normal in children, athletes, and pregnancy; in an adult over 40 it is the most specific sign of heart failure.

cards.front: When does S4 occur, what does it mean, and when is it impossible?
cards.back: Late diastole at the atrial kick, into a stiff ventricle. Cadence Ten-nes-see. Causes are hypertension, LVH, aortic stenosis, and ischemia. It cannot exist in atrial fibrillation.

cards.front: How do you position and listen to hear an S3 or S4?
cards.back: Bell pressed lightly at the apex with the patient rolled into left lateral decubitus. Pressing hard with the bell turns it into a diaphragm and the low-frequency sound disappears.

cards.front: What is a wide fixed split S2 and what causes it?
cards.back: An S2 split throughout the respiratory cycle with no variation. It is the classic sign of an atrial septal defect, because the shunt equalizes right-sided filling regardless of breathing.

cards.front: What is paradoxical splitting of S2 and what causes it?
cards.back: Splitting heard on expiration and single on inspiration, from delayed left ventricular emptying. Causes are left bundle branch block and severe aortic stenosis.

cards.front: What does the S2-to-opening-snap interval tell you in mitral stenosis?
cards.back: The shorter the interval, the higher the left atrial pressure and the more severe the stenosis, because a high atrial pressure forces the valve open sooner after S2.

cards.front: How do you distinguish a pericardial friction rub from a pleural rub?
cards.back: A pericardial rub continues when the patient holds their breath; a pleural rub stops. Listen at the left lower sternal border with the patient sitting forward at end-expiration.

cards.front: Define pulsus paradoxus and name its two main causes.
cards.back: A fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mmHg during inspiration. It points to cardiac tamponade or a severe asthma exacerbation.

cards.front: How is jugular venous pressure measured, and what is Kussmaul sign?
cards.back: Patient at 45 degrees; a column more than 3 cm above the sternal angle, about 8 cm H2O, is elevated. Kussmaul sign is a JVP that rises with inspiration, seen in constriction and right ventricular infarct.

cards.front: Why does reciprocal ST depression matter?
cards.back: It supports true coronary occlusion rather than a mimic. Pericarditis gives diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal change except in aVR.

cards.front: How does a posterior myocardial infarction appear on a standard 12-lead?
cards.back: As the mirror image in V1 to V3: ST depression, tall R waves, and upright T waves. Confirm with posterior leads V7 to V9, where 0.5 mm of elevation is diagnostic.

cards.front: How do you confirm right ventricular infarction, and what changes?
cards.back: 1 mm of ST elevation in V4R. Cardiac output becomes preload dependent, so nitroglycerin and morphine can cause profound hypotension and the treatment for hypotension is volume.

cards.front: What does diffuse ST depression with ST elevation in aVR suggest?
cards.back: Left main or severe three-vessel disease, or global subendocardial ischemia from any cause that starves the whole myocardium. It is a pattern of global supply-demand failure, not a single wall.

cards.front: What is Wellens syndrome and why does it matter?
cards.back: Deeply inverted or biphasic T waves in V2 and V3 while the patient is pain free, with preserved R waves and no Q waves. It means critical proximal LAD stenosis, and stress testing can infarct the patient.

cards.front: What is the de Winter pattern?
cards.back: Upsloping ST depression at the J point in the precordial leads with tall, symmetric, peaked T waves. It is treated as a proximal LAD occlusion equivalent despite the absence of ST elevation.

cards.front: State the Sgarbossa criteria and their point values.
cards.back: Concordant ST elevation of 1 mm or more scores 5, concordant ST depression of 1 mm or more in V1 to V3 scores 3, and excessively discordant elevation scores 2. The modified version uses an ST-to-S ratio of 0.25 or more.

cards.front: What are the ECG criteria for left and right ventricular hypertrophy?
cards.back: LVH: S in V1 plus R in V5 or V6 over 35 mm, often with a lateral strain pattern. RVH: R taller than S in V1 with right axis deviation.

cards.front: What are P pulmonale and P mitrale?
cards.back: P pulmonale is a tall peaked P over 2.5 mm in lead II, meaning right atrial enlargement. P mitrale is a wide notched P in lead II, meaning left atrial enlargement, as in mitral stenosis.

cards.front: Which ECG findings are normal training adaptations in an athlete?
cards.back: Sinus bradycardia into the 40s, sinus arrhythmia, first-degree AV block, Mobitz type I, early repolarization, and isolated voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy.

cards.front: Which ECG findings in an athlete are never normal?
cards.back: T-wave inversion beyond V1, ST depression, pathologic Q waves, complete left bundle branch block, QTc 470 ms or more in men or 480 ms or more in women, and any ventricular arrhythmia.

cards.front: What do FEV1, FVC, and their ratio measure?
cards.back: FVC is the total volume forcibly exhaled, FEV1 is how much came out in the first second, and the ratio is normally 75 to 80 percent in a healthy adult.

cards.front: What defines obstruction on spirometry and how is severity graded?
cards.back: A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70. Severity by FEV1 percent predicted: 80 or more mild, 50 to 79 moderate, 30 to 49 severe, under 30 very severe.

cards.front: What counts as a significant bronchodilator response?
cards.back: An increase in FEV1 or FVC of at least 12 percent AND at least 200 mL. A significant response points toward asthma; COPD improves incompletely or not at all.

cards.front: What does a restrictive pattern look like, and what actually confirms it?
cards.back: FEV1 and FVC both reduced with a normal or elevated ratio. Confirmation requires a total lung capacity below 80 percent predicted, since spirometry alone can be mimicked by poor effort.

cards.front: How does DLCO separate asthma from emphysema?
cards.back: Both are obstructive, but emphysema destroys alveolar capillary surface so DLCO is low, while asthma narrows airways without destroying membrane so DLCO is normal or high.

cards.front: How does DLCO separate the two kinds of restriction?
cards.back: Restriction with a low DLCO means the lung tissue itself is diseased, as in interstitial fibrosis. Restriction with a normal DLCO means the problem is outside the lung: obesity, kyphoscoliosis, or neuromuscular weakness.

cards.front: What does flattening of the inspiratory limb alone mean?
cards.back: Variable extrathoracic obstruction, classically vocal cord dysfunction, which is often misdiagnosed as refractory asthma. Both limbs flattened means a fixed lesion such as tracheal stenosis.

cards.front: How is peak expiratory flow used in an exacerbation?
cards.back: Compared with the patient's personal best, not a population value. Below 50 percent marks a severe exacerbation and below 33 percent is life-threatening. It is effort dependent and reflects large airways.

cards.front: What is the difference between volume control and pressure control ventilation?
cards.back: Volume control guarantees tidal volume, so worsening lungs appear as rising airway pressure. Pressure control guarantees inspiratory pressure, so worsening lungs appear as falling tidal volume.

cards.front: What happens when a tachypneic patient is on assist-control?
cards.back: Every triggered breath receives the full set tidal volume, so a patient triggering 35 times a minute gets 35 full breaths. That is how breath stacking and auto-PEEP begin.

cards.front: Give the standard initial ventilator settings.
cards.back: Tidal volume 6 to 8 mL/kg of predicted body weight, 6 mL/kg if ARDS is suspected; rate 12 to 16; PEEP 5 cm H2O; FiO2 100 percent then weaned to SpO2 92 to 96 percent.

cards.front: Why is tidal volume based on predicted rather than actual body weight?
cards.back: Lung size scales with height, not with adipose tissue. Using actual weight in an obese patient delivers a volume large enough to injure the lung.

cards.front: What are the two ventilator pressure safety limits?
cards.back: Plateau pressure under 30 cm H2O, and driving pressure, which is plateau minus PEEP, under about 15. These limits prevent ventilator-induced lung injury.

cards.front: How do you ventilate a severe asthmatic?
cards.back: Slow rate of 8 to 10, long expiratory time with I:E of 1:4 or 1:5, and permissive hypercapnia accepting a high CO2 as long as pH stays above roughly 7.20.

cards.front: An intubated asthmatic suddenly becomes hypotensive. What is the first maneuver?
cards.back: Disconnect from the ventilator and press on the chest to let the trapped air out. Breath stacking raises intrathoracic pressure until venous return fails, and disconnection reverses it in seconds.

cards.front: What does high peak pressure with a normal plateau pressure mean?
cards.back: A resistance problem: secretions, bronchospasm, a kinked or bitten tube. Plateau is measured during an inspiratory hold with no flow, so it isolates compliance.

cards.front: What does high peak AND high plateau pressure mean?
cards.back: A compliance problem: pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, ARDS, mainstem intubation, or abdominal distension. The lung or the chest has become stiff.

cards.front: What does DOPE stand for and what is the universal first response?
cards.back: Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment failure. Disconnect from the ventilator and hand-bag with 100 percent oxygen while someone listens, suctions, and checks capnography.

cards.front: How much fluid is in a normal pleural space and what does it do?
cards.back: 10 to 20 mL. Surface tension in that film couples lung to chest wall, so the chest wall's outward spring holds the lung open against its own elastic recoil.

cards.front: How much pleural fluid does it take to see an effusion, by film and by ultrasound?
cards.back: Roughly 200 to 500 mL to blunt the costophrenic angle on an upright film; about 50 mL on ultrasound. A supine film hides it as a hazy hemithorax.

cards.front: State Light's criteria.
cards.back: Exudate if any one holds: pleural-to-serum protein ratio over 0.5, pleural-to-serum LDH ratio over 0.6, or pleural LDH over two thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH.

cards.front: When does a parapneumonic effusion require drainage?
cards.back: pH below 7.20, glucose below 60 mg/dL, LDH above 1000, a positive Gram stain or culture, or frank pus. Empyema is not cured by antibiotics alone.

cards.front: How much fluid can be removed at one thoracentesis, and why the limit?
cards.back: About 1.5 L. Draining a chronically collapsed lung faster causes re-expansion pulmonary edema, whose first sign is usually cough during the procedure.

cards.front: Who gets a primary versus a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax?
cards.back: Primary: tall thin young people, usually smokers, from ruptured apical blebs. Secondary: patients with existing lung disease such as COPD, and far more dangerous because there is no reserve.

cards.front: What actually kills in a tension pneumothorax?
cards.back: Obstructive shock. A one-way flap raises intrathoracic pressure until the vena cava kinks and venous return stops. Hypotension and distended neck veins matter more than the oxygen saturation.

cards.front: Where do you needle a tension pneumothorax, and what follows?
cards.back: 2nd intercostal space at the midclavicular line, or the 5th intercostal space at the anterior axillary line, which is preferred in adults for a thinner chest wall. A chest tube follows regardless.

cards.front: How fast does a small pneumothorax resorb, and how does oxygen help?
cards.back: About 1 to 2 percent of the hemithorax per day on room air. High-flow oxygen speeds it several times over by washing nitrogen out of blood and steepening the gradient pulling trapped nitrogen back in.

cards.front: What defines pulmonary hypertension now, and what changed?
cards.back: A mean pulmonary artery pressure above 20 mmHg at rest, lowered from the older threshold of 25 mmHg. Precapillary disease also requires an elevated pulmonary vascular resistance.

cards.front: Name the five WHO groups of pulmonary hypertension.
cards.back: 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension, 2 left heart disease and the most common, 3 lung disease and hypoxia, 4 chronic thromboembolic disease, 5 multifactorial.

cards.front: Why does the right ventricle fail so quickly when afterload rises?
cards.back: It is a thin crescent built to move a large volume against about one sixth of left-sided pressure. It has no muscle mass in reserve, so a sudden afterload load fails it within minutes.

cards.front: Describe the right ventricular failure death spiral.
cards.back: RV dilates, the septum bows into the LV, LV filling and systemic pressure fall, right coronary perfusion falls, the RV becomes ischemic and fails harder, and the loop closes.

cards.front: Which three physiologic states raise pulmonary vascular resistance and must be corrected?
cards.back: Hypoxia, hypercapnia, and acidosis. All three constrict the pulmonary vasculature and worsen the afterload you are trying to reduce.

cards.front: How are fluids and pressors used in right ventricular failure?
cards.back: Fluids in small 250 mL boluses, because a large bolus overstretches the RV and worsens septal bowing. Norepinephrine early, because systemic pressure is the RV's coronary perfusion pressure.

cards.front: What are the bedside signs of cor pulmonale?
cards.back: Jugular venous distension, a parasternal right ventricular heave, a loud P2, a tricuspid regurgitation murmur louder with inspiration, hepatomegaly with a pulsatile liver, ascites, and dependent edema.

cards.front: Name two absolute medication rules in pulmonary hypertension.
cards.back: Never interrupt a continuous intravenous prostacyclin, since the half-life is minutes and rebound can be fatal. Never combine a PDE-5 inhibitor with nitrates, which causes profound hypotension.

cards.front: How do acyanotic and cyanotic congenital lesions differ?
cards.back: Acyanotic lesions shunt left to right, causing pulmonary overcirculation, heart failure, and failure to thrive without cyanosis. Cyanotic lesions shunt right to left, so oxygen cannot correct the saturation.

cards.front: Describe the murmurs of VSD, ASD, and PDA.
cards.back: VSD: harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, louder when the hole is smaller. ASD: soft pulmonic ejection murmur with a wide fixed split S2. PDA: continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle.

cards.front: How does coarctation of the aorta present?
cards.back: Upper extremity hypertension with weak, delayed femoral pulses and a palpable radiofemoral delay. It is associated with bicuspid aortic valve and Turner syndrome.

cards.front: Name the five cyanotic lesions and the four features of tetralogy of Fallot.
cards.back: The five T's: Tetralogy, Transposition, Truncus arteriosus, Total anomalous pulmonary venous return, Tricuspid atresia. Tetralogy is pulmonic stenosis, RV hypertrophy, overriding aorta, and a VSD.

cards.front: What is a tet spell and how is it treated?
cards.back: A hypercyanotic episode where falling systemic resistance increases right-to-left shunting; the murmur gets quieter. Treat by raising systemic resistance: knees to chest, oxygen, calming, morphine, fluids, phenylephrine.

cards.front: What is a ductal-dependent lesion and what drug is used?
